title: Seeking Time to Produce Papers Isn't Admitting Illegal Construction: Calcutta High Court
meta_description: Calcutta High Court quashes a Howrah demolition order, holding a letter seeking time to submit documents is not an admission of unauthorised construction.
case_name: Sujoy Sarkar @ Sujay Sarkar v. Howrah Municipal Corporation & Others
body: Sujoy Sarkar, also described in the case papers as Sujay Sarkar, had a demolition order served on him by the Assistant Engineer of the Howrah Municipal Corporation, dated 28 September 2026. With enforcement of that order looming, he moved the Calcutta High Court against it, and the matter came up before a vacation bench rather than waiting for the Court to resume its regular sittings.

The Corporation's case for demolition rested almost entirely on a letter Sarkar himself had written, dated 3 April 2025, well over a year before the demolition order itself was passed. The civic body read that letter as an admission that the construction on his property was unauthorised, and built its entire demolition order on that one document, without pointing to any independent inspection report or fresh finding of illegality.

Sarkar's side disputed that the letter said any such thing. All it did, they argued, was ask the Corporation for time to collect and put in documents relating to the construction. A request for more time to produce papers is not the same thing as admitting there is something wrong with what was built, and nothing in the letter went further than that. Treating the two as equivalent, the argument ran, let the Corporation skip the actual work of establishing illegality and jump straight to demolition on the strength of an admission that existed only in its own reading of the letter.

Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya, sitting as a vacation bench, went through the letter himself rather than accepting the Corporation's characterisation of it. He found it contained no admission at all about the construction being unauthorised. Sarkar had only asked for more time to submit his papers concerning the construction. Once that was clear, the entire premise on which the Corporation had built its demolition order no longer held up, because there was no other material on record showing the construction to be illegal.

The Court accordingly set aside the demolition order of 28 September 2026. Sarkar was given a fresh opportunity to place his supporting documents before the Corporation, something the underlying letter had itself asked permission to do close to eighteen months earlier. The Howrah Municipal Corporation was directed to consider those documents and pass a fresh, reasoned order within eight weeks of receiving them, rather than act again on the same mistaken reading of the April 2025 letter.

That said, the judgment was careful to add that the High Court itself was not deciding whether the construction is in fact authorised. That question stays open for the Corporation to examine properly, on the material Sarkar now puts before it, rather than on an admission that the letter never actually contained. The owner gets a fresh hearing on the merits, not a final clearance of the construction.

Demolition is a drastic step against a standing structure, and courts have long expected civic bodies to get the factual basis for it right before they act, rather than after a structure has already come down. This order adds a specific and useful line to that requirement: a property owner's request for time to gather documents cannot, without more, be read as a concession that the documents would show illegality. The distinction matters because once a demolition order is carried out, there is no undoing it, and a civic body that skips the step of actually establishing illegality, relying instead on a stretched reading of the owner's own letter, leaves its order exposed exactly as the Howrah Corporation's was here.

For municipal corporations across the Kolkata region, including Howrah and the areas under the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, the lesson is a narrow but practical one. Correspondence from a property owner asking for time has to be read for what it actually says, not stretched into an admission that makes the Corporation's job easier. A civic body that wants to demolish a structure still has to show, on its own inspection or on some other independent material, that the construction is unauthorised, rather than lean on a letter that only ever asked for more time.
why_it_matters: Municipal demolition orders in West Bengal are frequently built on the owner's own correspondence with the civic body. This ruling tells municipal corporations, including the Howrah and Kolkata authorities, that they cannot stretch an ordinary request for more time into an admission of illegal construction, and that owners facing demolition on that basis have a real ground to challenge the order and get a fresh, reasoned decision.
card_summary: Calcutta High Court quashes a Howrah Municipal Corporation demolition order, holding the owner's letter asking for time to submit documents was not an admission that his construction was illegal.
card_tip: If a demolition notice treats your request for time to submit documents as an admission of illegal construction, check the actual wording of what you wrote before accepting the order.
verification_notes: The case name, writ petition number (WPA 31462 of 2026), the 10 November 2026 decision date, the judge's name, the underlying 28 September 2026 demolition order, the 3 April 2025 letter, the holding, and the eight-week direction are confirmed across LiveLaw's report and LawChakra's report, which agree on the case number, date, and outcome; an Indian Kanoon docket entry for the same case name and date was also located. LiveLaw describes the bench as a vacation bench while another report calls it a single-judge order; this draft follows LiveLaw's description. The Court's observation that it has not ruled on the legality of the construction itself is stated in the LiveLaw report and is carried through here as an express limit on the ruling.
